continuity_scope: A deliberately bounded reference pass within living, iwi- and hapū-specific Māori oral, performed, manuscript, and published traditions in Aotearoa. This is not a pan-Māori definitive canon. The selected witnesses are Te Ara sections that explicitly identify their regional/informant framing where supplied: a Ngāti Raukawa creation example; a Ngāti Porou Māui account; a Te Rangihaeata (Ngāti Toarangatira) land-form account; and Heretaunga and Wairoa taniwha accounts. Te Ara's comparative summaries are used as published reference witnesses, not as substitutes for community authority or for all local variants.

coverage_rule: Include only named agents who materially act in one of the selected published witness episodes: the named earth-sky family and human-origin episode; Māui’s fishing episode; the named freshwater taniwha episodes; and the explicitly witnessed Hinetītama/Hine-nui-te-pō change. Do not turn generic atua, taniwha, whakapapa, ritual concepts, places, unnamed relatives, unnamed brothers, or present-day communities into character nodes. Names and forms follow the cited Te Ara witness; regional variants are not merged or silently generalized.
omissions: All unnamed children of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, Māui’s unnamed brothers, and unnamed human canoe travellers
Other named figures merely enumerated as domain associations without material action in the selected episode
All other iwi, hapū, rohe, whānau, manuscript, oral-performance, ritual, historical, and contemporary witnesses not listed above
Io traditions, whose status and history Te Ara identifies as debated
Generic atua, taniwha, tipua, whakapapa, mana, tapu, noa, karakia, places, and collective communities, which remain terms rather than characters
uncertainties: Spellings, identities, genealogical positions, roles, and narrative details vary by iwi, hapū, narrator, manuscript, language practice, and published edition; this pass does not adjudicate among them.
Te Ara's English comparison words such as ‘god’, ‘trickster hero’, ‘monster’, ‘dragon’, ‘creation’, and ‘transformation’ are not claims that Māori terms are generic fantasy categories.

The selected Te Ara pages describe published accounts and their cited sources; they do not grant authority to reproduce, interpret, or practise mātauranga, tikanga, karakia, or whakapapa outside appropriate relationships and contexts.
evidence_basis: Claim-specific records cite the exact Te Ara story page and named section/paragraph. Te Ara is an authoritative public encyclopedia, and its pages preserve the stated regional or named-source framing where relevant. This pass is complete only for the exact selected Te Ara reference episodes, counts, and coverage rule; it is not a claim of completion for living, diverse Māori traditions or any unselected iwi/hapū witness.

citations.locator: ‘Common threads in creation stories’, §§ ‘Themes in Māori creation myths’ and ‘The separation of earth and sky’, paras. 1–2
supports: Creation accounts have shared threads but considerable diversity among tribal versions.
Ranginui, Papatūānuku, their children, and the separation are presented as a creation narrative in the bounded witness.
The selected Māui account is attributed to Ngāti Porou tohunga Mohi Ruatapu and records Māui’s fishing episode.

citations.locator: ‘The North and South islands’, §§ ‘Māui fishes up the North Island’ and ‘How the North Island got its shape’, paras. 1–3
supports: The page identifies a Te Rangihaeata/Ngāti Toarangatira version and records regional differences in the land-form account.

citations.locator: ‘Freshwater taniwha’, §§ ‘Lake Roto-a-Tara’ and ‘Te Rēinga waterfall’, paras. 1–2
supports: The selected freshwater episodes name Te Tau-a-Porirua and Tara, and Hine-kōrako and Tāne-kino.
The source-term entries for mana, tapu, and noa are grounded in a specific published reference section.
